1058.title: How many gods?
1058.hook: a sage at King Janaka's court is asked how many gods there are, and counts down from thousands to one
1058.howItsDone: Many Hindus explain their many gods with the Rig Veda's line ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti, and many families keep several deities side by side in one home shrine.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Nasadiya Sukta, the hymn of creation that ends with or perhaps not. A question can stay open.

A king named Janaka pens up a thousand cows, with gold tied to their horns, and announces: these go to the wisest one here. Nobody dares move, except a sage named Yajnavalkya, who calmly tells his student: drive them home. The court erupts. One by one, the learned stand up to test him. Near the end comes Shakalya, and his question is one Hindu kids still get asked at lunch tables: how many gods are there?
screen: `A THOUSAND COWS, GOLD ON THEIR HORNS.` → `DRIVE THEM HOME.` → `HOW MANY GODS ARE THERE?`

segments.voice: The story is in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. Yajnavalkya answers: three thousand three hundred and six. Shakalya says, yes, but how many, really? Thirty-three. Yes, but really? Six. Three. Two. One and a half. And at last: one. Which is the one god? The breath, Yajnavalkya says. It is Brahman, and they call it simply: that. Here's the teaching under the count. Hindus honor many gods, Ganesha, Lakshmi, Shiva, the goddess, and many Hindus understand them as faces of one reality, Brahman. An older line in the Rig Veda says it in a breath: ekam sat, the one that is, vipra bahudha vadanti, the sages call by many names. Not every Hindu reads that the same way. Some worship one god, Vishnu or Shiva or the Devi, as supreme, and see the others as that god's forms or helpers. Others understand Brahman as beyond every form at all. And next year, the schools of thought take the question one at a time. They're called darshanas, and darshana means seeing, the same word as darshan at a temple, when you go to see the deity. Each school is a way of seeing the one and the many, and their teachers argued, sometimes sharply. So when a friend asks how many gods Hindus have, there's an old answer from Janaka's court: count as high as you like; Yajnavalkya came down to one.
screen: `3,306. 33. 6. 3. 2. ONE AND A HALF. ONE.` · `THE ONE: BRAHMAN, CALLED 'THAT'.` · `EKAM SAT: ONE, CALLED BY MANY NAMES.` · `DARSHANA: A WAY OF SEEING.` · then, large: `MANY NAMES, ONE REALITY.`

segments.voice: Hindus have whole hymns that are nothing but names of God. Try three. Choose names your family uses, maybe Ram, Krishna, Ma, Shiva, and say one slowly with each breath out. After each name, rest in the quiet that follows; notice it's the same quiet after every name. If you pray, let the last name be the one closest to you; if you don't, say three things you love instead, and notice the one attention underneath them.
Darshana. A way of seeing: the word for each school of thought ahead, and the same word as darshan at a temple. Many ways of seeing, one reality seen.
Your line: many names, one reality. Yajnavalkya counted down from thousands to one. I'll be here tomorrow.

1059.title: The lump of clay
1059.hook: a young man comes home from his studies proud, and his father asks one question he can't answer
1059.carry: one clay under every name and form
1059.howItsDone: The dialogue between Uddalaka and Shvetaketu in the Chandogya Upanishad is taught in Vedanta as the setting of the saying tat tvam asi, and some Hindu teachers retell it as a lesson in a student's humility.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yajnavalkya counted the gods down to one: many names, one reality.

A son walks back into his father's house after years away at study. He has learned the Vedas. He carries himself like someone who has finished. The Chandogya Upanishad doesn't flatter him: it says he came home proud, thinking himself learned. His father, Uddalaka, asks one question, and the son, Shvetaketu, who knows so much, has no idea what his father means. Year two walked through this scene. It comes back today, one day before the year closes, as the doorway to the last of the ranges ahead: the great sayings.
screen: `HOME FROM STUDY, PROUD.` → `ONE QUESTION FROM HIS FATHER.` → `NO IDEA WHAT HE MEANS.`

segments.voice: Here's the question, in paraphrase: did you ask for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known? Shvetaketu says, sir, what kind of teaching is that? So his father gives him a picture. By knowing one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. The pot, the cup, the lamp: the difference is a name, a way of speaking. What's real is the clay. Then comes the line that makes the scene. Shvetaketu says, in effect: surely my teachers didn't know this, or why wouldn't they have told me? Teach me, sir. He came home finished. One question later, he's a beginner again. What follows is a long teaching. In the beginning, the father says, there was only being, sat, one without a second. And again and again he ends with a short phrase: tat tvam asi, that you are. Tradition counts it among the great sayings. Here's the teaching, plainly. Vedanta calls that one being Brahman: the clay under every name and form, under the many gods of yesterday, and under you. And it isn't gathered like facts. It's asked for, humbly, from a teacher, which is why Hindus honor the guru, and why even a proud graduate starts again with: teach me, sir.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing this path taught you this year, a story, a line, a practice, and hold it up like the lump of clay. Don't recite it; ask what's underneath it that you haven't heard yet, then set it down and simply breathe, with nothing finished. If you pray, you can bring the words teach me to God in your own way; if you don't, let the question stay with you through the sit.

Your line: one clay under every name and form. The proud graduate became a beginner, and that was the start. Year three is nearly done.

1060.title: The most wonderful thing
1060.hook: the year's summit sit: Yudhishthira at the lake, and the wonder of how the living forget death
1060.howItsDone: Yudhishthira's answers to the yaksha in the Mahabharata's Vana Parva are retold in Hindu homes and talks, and in Pitru Paksha, the fortnight before Navaratri, many families offer water, sesame and food in memory of their ancestors.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shvetaketu, home and proud, who became a beginner again with teach me, sir.

Day six hundred ninety-seven: a king's snake sacrifice, and a storyteller who begins the story of the Bharatas. That's where this year started. Since then: a war, a song, a child in Vraja, the saints. Today, the summit sit, and one scene. Five brothers in the forest, desperately thirsty. One finds a lake. A voice from the water says: answer my questions first, then drink. He drinks anyway, and falls. So does the next brother, and the next, and the next.
screen: `DAY 697: THE SNAKE SACRIFICE.` → `A LAKE IN THE FOREST.` → `ANSWER FIRST, THEN DRINK.`

segments.voice: Then the eldest, Yudhishthira, reaches the shore and finds his four brothers lying still. He doesn't drink. He says: ask. The voice, a yaksha, a spirit of the lake, asks question after question. One of them: what is the most wonderful thing? His answer, in paraphrase: every day, living beings go to the house of Death, and the ones who remain want to stay forever. What could be more wonderful than that? His wonder isn't at death. It's at forgetting: we see it every day and live as if it isn't coming. Then the yaksha offers him one brother back, his choice. He picks Nakula, a son of his father's other wife, not mighty Bhima or Arjuna, so that Madri, too, will have a living son, as his own mother Kunti does. And the yaksha shows who he is: Dharma himself, Yudhishthira's own father, testing him. He gives all four brothers back. Here's the teaching. In Hindu thought the body is passing, and dharma, right living, is what you do with the time; remembering death isn't gloom, it's what makes the right choice clear. Hindu families build that remembering into the year. Just before Navaratri comes Pitru Paksha, a fortnight for the ancestors, when many families offer water, sesame and food in memory of those who have gone, often with a share set out for the crows. The living forget, Yudhishthira said; these days are for not forgetting.
screen: `FOUR BROTHERS, LYING STILL.` · `WHAT IS THE MOST WONDERFUL THING?` · `HE CHOOSES NAKULA.` · `THE VOICE WAS DHARMA.` · `PITRU PAKSHA: DAYS TO REMEMBER.` · then, large: `WE REMAIN ONLY FOR NOW.`

segments.voice: Hold a glass of water. Families who keep Pitru Paksha may know tarpan, water offered in memory of those who have gone; this is a small way in its spirit. Bring one person to mind, from your family or your life, say their name, and pour a little of the water into a plant or onto the earth. Notice the breath still coming: you remain, for now. If you pray, give thanks for them in words you already use; if you don't, let the water be the thanks. If a loss ever feels too heavy to carry alone, in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.
Year three. The great story, the child in Vraja, the saints and the teachers, held together by the ones who remain.

1061.title: No effort is lost
1061.hook: Arjuna asks what happens to someone who starts the path and drifts off it, and Krishna answers
1061.carry: no effort on the path is lost, even across lives
1061.howItsDone: Bhagavad Gita 2.40 and 6.40 are quoted by Hindu teachers to encourage people who are starting a practice or returning to one, as a promise that sincere effort on the path is not wasted.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the lake, and Yudhishthira's wonder that the living forget: we remain only for now.
screen: `THE MOST WONDERFUL THING.` · `WE REMAIN ONLY FOR NOW.`

segments.voice: In the sixth chapter of the Gita, Krishna has been describing the steady yogi, the one who sits still and sees the same Self in every being. And Arjuna, honest as ever, says: my mind is restless, Krishna. Holding it is like trying to hold the wind. Then he asks the question every beginner asks. What about the one who has faith, who starts, and whose mind wanders off the path before the end? Is he lost both ways, like a torn cloud in the sky, nothing here, nothing there?
screen: `MY MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.` → `WHAT IF I DRIFT OFF THE PATH?` → `A TORN CLOUD?`

segments.voice: Krishna's answer is a much-loved passage. In paraphrase: no, Arjuna. Neither in this world nor the next is that person destroyed; no one who does good comes to a bad end. After a long stay in good worlds, Krishna says, they're born again into a pure and prosperous home, or even into a family of wise yogis. And there they pick up the understanding they had before, and strive again. Here's the Hindu teaching underneath, plainly. Karma: what you do leaves an imprint, and the imprint of practice is kept. And rebirth: in Hindu belief the self goes on through many lives, so a path begun isn't canceled when a body ends. The Gita says it earlier too, in the second chapter: on this path no effort begun is lost, and even a little of this dharma protects from great fear. Some teachers read that generously: the half-managed sit, the missed week, the prayer you used to know by heart. Others hear it more strictly, about the yoga Krishna is teaching. Either way, it's why a Hindu grandparent might tell a child who forgot the aarti that it isn't gone; it's in you, waiting to be picked up. Year three ends here: a war, a song, a child, the saints, the teachers, and every sit you managed, kept. Tomorrow year four begins with the goddess.
screen: `NO ONE WHO DOES GOOD COMES TO A BAD END.` · `BORN AGAIN, HE STRIVES AGAIN.` · `KARMA KEEPS THE PRACTICE.` · `EVEN A LITTLE PROTECTS.` · then, large: `NO EFFORT ON THE PATH IS LOST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing of your faith you once knew and let slip: a prayer, an aarti, a story, the habit of lighting a lamp. Don't scold yourself. Say or hum the part you still remember, even one line, and let that be the next step, picked up where it was left. If you pray, offer that line to God in your own way; if you don't, let one small practice from this year come back for a breath or two.

Your line: no effort on the path is lost, even across lives. Krishna told Arjuna so. Year three, done.

1062.title: Why doesn't knowing help?
1062.hook: a king who has lost everything and a merchant thrown out by his own family meet in a forest, and neither can stop worrying
1062.carry: the goddess who binds the mind, and frees it
1062.tomorrow: The goddess who is Vishnu's sleep
1062.howItsDone: Some Hindus recite the Devi Mahatmya, also called the Chandi or Durga Saptashati, from beginning to end, especially during Navaratri, and it is recited in some temples devoted to the goddess.

segments.voice: Yesterday, year three closed with Krishna's promise: no effort on the path is lost. Year four begins with the goddess.

A king rides into a forest alone, his kingdom lost. Enemies beat him in battle, then his own ministers turned on him and took the treasury. He finds the quiet hermitage of a sage named Medhas, and stays. And under the trees he can't stop worrying. Is my elephant fed? Are my servants treated well? Is my treasure being wasted? Then he meets a merchant named Samadhi, sitting there just as lost. That's how the Devi Mahatmya begins, and year four reads it whole.
screen: `A KING RIDES INTO A FOREST ALONE.` → `HE CAN'T STOP WORRYING.` → `A MERCHANT, JUST AS LOST.`

segments.voice: Devi Mahatmya means the glory of the goddess. Tradition places it inside the Markandeya Purana; it's also called the Chandi, and some homes and temples recite it whole. Yet it opens with no goddess at all. The merchant's is the harder one. His own wife and sons, greedy for his money, threw him out. And still he can't stop wondering whether they're well. So they bring the sage one honest question. In paraphrase: we know these things have left us. So why do we still grieve? Why doesn't knowing help? Medhas doesn't call them foolish. He points at birds: hungry themselves, they still drop grain into the beaks of their young. Every creature, he says, is pulled this way. Then he names the pull: Mahamaya, the great illusion, and in this text she is the goddess herself. She seizes the minds of even the wise and drags them into confusion. And the same goddess, when gracious, sets people free. That's the surprise, and the teaching. For Shakta Hindus, who worship the goddess as supreme, she is Shakti, the power behind everything: even the pull these men carried into the forest, and the freedom from it. That's why her devotees pray to her for release, not only for help. The king asks: who is this goddess? Medhas answers with stories, and the rest of the book is those stories.
screen: `TWO MEN WITH A PROBLEM.` · `WHY DOESN'T KNOWING HELP?` · `MAHAMAYA BINDS, AND SETS FREE.` · `SHAKTI: THE POWER BEHIND IT ALL.` · then, large: `WHO IS THIS GODDESS?`

segments.voice: Let one thing your mind keeps going back to come up on its own, a person, a place, something gone that still pulls, and notice the pull the way the merchant noticed his, without arguing or fixing. With each breath out, let the grip loosen a little; if you pray, hold it before God or the goddess in your own words, and if you don't, let the breath do the holding. If that pull is ever too heavy to carry alone, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.
The Devi Mahatmya. The glory of the goddess: a book that begins in a forest, with two worried men and a sage who names the pull.

1063.title: The goddess who is Vishnu's sleep
1063.hook: the first story: Vishnu asleep on the waters, two demons rising, and Brahma praising the goddess who is Vishnu's sleep
1063.carry: the goddess's power moves even the gods
1063.howItsDone: Brahma's praise of Yoganidra in the first chapter of the Devi Mahatmya is recited as part of the whole text, and some Hindus who recite the Chandi treat the first chapter as its own opening section.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Devi Mahatmya opened in a forest: two worried men, and the goddess who binds the mind, and frees it.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `TWO MEN IN A FOREST.`

segments.voice: No land. Only water, everywhere, at the end of an age. On it Vishnu lies asleep on the great serpent. From his navel grows a lotus, and on it sits Brahma, the creator. Then, out of the dirt in Vishnu's ears, two demons are born: Madhu and Kaitabha. They see Brahma on his flower and decide to kill him. Brahma looks down at Vishnu, the one who could protect him. Vishnu doesn't move. This is the sage Medhas's first story, and the goddess is in it from the start, though not where you'd look.
screen: `ONLY WATER, AT THE END OF AN AGE.` → `TWO DEMONS RISE.` → `VISHNU WON'T WAKE.`

segments.voice: Brahma doesn't shake Vishnu or call his name. He turns to the sleep itself. Here Vishnu's sleep has a name, Yoganidra, and she is the goddess. So Brahma praises her. In paraphrase: you hold up this world, create it, protect it, and at the end take it back. You are the great knowledge and the great illusion, the dark night at the end of things, and beauty, modesty and understanding. Who could praise you enough, when you put even Vishnu to sleep? Then a request: wake him, and confuse these two demons. The goddess answers, drawing out of Vishnu's eyes, mouth, nostrils, arms, heart and chest. Vishnu wakes and fights them for a very long time. Then the strangest moment. Confused by the great illusion and proud of their strength, the demons tell Vishnu they're pleased with him: ask us a boon. He asks: be killable by me. Caught, they look at the water everywhere and add a condition: then kill us where the earth isn't covered with water. Vishnu lifts them onto his thigh, dry ground above the flood, and kills them there. So the goddess isn't a helper standing beside Vishnu. She's the power inside his sleeping and his waking. That's the teaching of this book, named plainly: Shakti, the goddess, is the power that moves even the gods; without her, many devotees say, even the greatest god lies still. And yesterday's confusion is at work in the demons: outwitted by their own pride.
screen: `BRAHMA PRAISES THE SLEEP ITSELF.` · `THE GODDESS LEAVES VISHNU'S EYES.` · `NO DRY LAND? HIS THIGH.` · `SHAKTI MOVES EVEN THE GODS.` · then, large: `EVEN VISHNU RESTS IN HER.`

segments.voice: Close the eyes and follow the order the text gives as the goddess leaves Vishnu: let attention wake in the eyes behind the lids, then the mouth, the nose and its breath, the arms, the heart, the chest, one place at a time, without forcing. If you pray, greet the goddess by a name your family uses, Durga, Amba, Ma; if not, let the breath be the greeting.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, its first story: the goddess as Yoganidra, the sleep of Vishnu, who leaves him so he can wake.
Your line: the goddess's power moves even the gods. In this book, even Vishnu's sleep is Shakti. See you tomorrow.

1064.title: Why Durga has many arms
1064.hook: the second story begins: every god gives the goddess something of his own, and the mountain gives her a lion
1064.carry: every god's power, held by one goddess
1064.tomorrow: The demon who keeps changing shape
1064.howItsDone: Images of Durga in temples and in festival pandals during Navaratri and Durga Puja can show her many arms holding the weapons the gods gave her, riding a lion, as told in the Devi Mahatmya's second chapter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vishnu slept on the waters until Brahma praised the goddess who was his sleep: the goddess's power moves even the gods.

A trident. A discus. A conch. A spear. A bow and two quivers of arrows. A thunderbolt, and a bell from an elephant's neck. A staff. A noose. Prayer beads and a water pot. A sword and a shield. An axe. Jewels, and a garland that never fades. A drinking cup. A snake to wear around the neck. And a lion. That's the inventory of the Devi Mahatmya's second story. It begins with the gods beaten by the buffalo demon Mahisha, their anger pouring out as light, and the light becoming a goddess. So what does everyone give her?
screen: `A TRIDENT, A DISCUS, A CONCH.` → `A CUP, A SNAKE, A LION.` → `WHAT DOES EVERYONE GIVE HER?`

segments.voice: In the second chapter the gods line up to give, and each gift comes out of the giver's own thing. Shiva draws a trident from his trident. Vishnu brings a discus out of his discus. Varuna gives a conch and a noose. Agni, fire, gives a spear. Indra gives a thunderbolt from his own, and a bell from his elephant. Brahma gives prayer beads and a water pot. The sun fills the pores of her skin with his rays. Kubera, lord of wealth, gives a full drinking cup. And Himavat, the Himalaya itself, gives her a lion to ride. Notice the first gifts. Shiva, Vishnu and Indra don't hand over a spare; each draws a copy from his own power. She carries all of it at once. That's why the goddess Hindus know as Durga is shown with many arms, each hand holding a god's gift, riding a lion: for devotees she is the gods' combined power in one form. Then she laughs, long and loud, and the sky fills with the sound. The earth shakes, and the demons rush toward the noise and see her, filling the three worlds with light. Mahisha's generals come at her with armies. As she fights, the breaths she lets out become troops, beating drums and blowing conches. She breathes, and allies appear. Her lion stalks through the enemy, and the chapter ends with the armies in ruins, and Mahisha still to come.
screen: `EACH GIFT FROM THE GIVER'S OWN.` · `THE MOUNTAIN GIVES A LION.` · `MANY ARMS, EVERY GOD'S GIFT.` · `HER BREATHS BECOME ARMIES.` · then, large: `SHE CARRIES ALL OF IT AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Find an image of Durga, in a home shrine, on your phone, or in your mind. Look at it slowly, hand by hand: the trident, Shiva's; the discus, Vishnu's; the conch, Varuna's; and under her, the mountain's lion. Then take her in whole, all of it at once. Hindus call this darshan: seeing the deity, and, many say, being seen. If you pray, greet her in your own words; if you don't, simply look.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, its second story: a goddess armed with each god's own gift, riding the mountain's lion, whose breaths become armies.
Your line: every god's power, held by one goddess. Each gave from his own. That's today, done.
